summary: Port reproduces the original's three additively-blended red/green/blue balls bouncing in a box — identical blob profile, identical wall bounds, identical dial behaviour — but its randomly chosen ball speeds run faster and spread roughly twice as wide, and its motion is tied to real elapsed time where the original's is a fixed step per frame.
observations: Both sides render three soft radial blobs, one pure red, one pure green, one pure blue, additively combined on the default 16x16 grid; no runtime or compile errors on either side, both alive for the whole window (zeroMotionFrames = 1 on both, the unavoidable first frame).

Blob rendering is a near-exact match. Row through a red ball's peak at default BallRadius — orig: 65,104,151,207,231,173,122,79,46,21,6,0...; port: ...,12,32,61,99,146,201,234,178,127,83,49,24,7. Same soft falloff, same width, same ~230-255 peak (dump 'track').
Bounce bounds match: on both sides each ball's brightness centroid travels between 1.0 and 14.0 px in x and y on the 16x16 grid, i.e. the same wall inset (dump 'track', 24 consecutive frames).

Both sides are a SINGLE regime — no modes, no palette walk, no re-randomisation. Over 1200 frames (60 s @ 20 fps) every channel's frame-mean is strictly periodic (orig: G period 12, B period 30, mean abs residual <0.01; port: R period 6, G 15, B 60, residual <0.02). The survey rhythm images are homogeneous end to end on both sides, and the t=40-46 s contact sheets look like the t=0-6 s ones.

Ball speed distribution differs. Measured as the median per-frame centroid step of each ball, over 21 seeds x 3 balls = 63 balls per side, default dials, default rig, 20 fps: ORIG min 0.72 / p25 1.95 / median 2.91 / p75 3.51 / max 4.35 px per frame; PORT min 1.39 / p25 2.16 / median 3.27 / p75 4.56 / max 8.32 px per frame. 21 of 63 port balls (33%) are faster than anything the original ever produced, and the port never produced one of the original's slow drifters (12 of 63 orig balls are below the port's floor of 1.39).

That shows up in the aggregate motion stat consistently: orig 20.3 / 20.5 / 21 against port 25.5 / 25.8 / 26 for the 6 s baseline, the 60 s window and the 30 s skip-10 window respectively. Mean brightness is a match throughout (orig 21.8-21.9, port 21.3-21.4).

The port's fastest balls read as teleporting rather than gliding. In the frame-to-frame filmstrips both sides jump noticeably, but the port's top-end ball crosses about half the panel per frame (8.3 px on a 16 px grid) where the original's ceiling is about a quarter (4.35 px).

Motion is frame-rate-coupled on the port and not on the original. At the same frame index the original's output is bit-identical at 10, 20 and 40 fps (per-ball px/frame [1.51, 4.27, 3.99] at all three), i.e. a fixed step per rendered frame; the port's per-ball px/frame goes [17.08, 9.83, 2.65] at 10 fps, [7.64, 5.04, 1.26] at 20 fps, [4.53, 2.60, 0.55] at 40 fps, i.e. constant px/second. They are in the same ballpark only near 20 fps; at 40 fps the original moves ~2x further per frame than the port and at 10 fps ~2x less.

Consequence visible in the mandated 5 fps survey: the original still draws clean zigzag bounce traces in orig-rhythm.png while the port's rhythm collapses to flat horizontal bands, with its red frame-mean pinned at a constant value for all 300 frames — the port's balls have aliased into an exact per-frame cycle at that step size. This is the frame-rate coupling above, not a dead port; at 20 fps the same 60 s window is healthy.
Colour balance is comparable — over 60 frames spread across 60 s, orig mean RGB 23.0/21.2/21.5, port 19.2/21.3/22.8, and neither side produces saturated-white overlap pixels in that sample.

Control surface matches exactly: both sides expose sliderBallRadius (slider, label 'BallRadius') and sliderBallSpeed (slider, label 'BallSpeed'); the probe calls both responsive on both sides with near-identical magnitudes (radius maxDelta 43.82 orig / 43.57 port; speed 36.05 / 36.36).

dials.name: sliderBallRadius
dials.origEffect: 0 = output entirely black (frame mean 0, motion 0); 0.5 (default) = blobs with ~19 px above half-max, frame mean 22; 1 = blobs with ~69 px above half-max, frame mean 66. Continuous size knob, brightness rises with it.
dials.portEffect: Same: 0 = entirely black; 0.5 = ~19 px above half-max, frame mean 22; 1 = ~67 px above half-max, frame mean 65. Same direction, same magnitude, same black-at-zero endpoint.

dials.name: sliderBallSpeed
dials.origEffect: 0 = balls still drawn but completely frozen (motion 0, frame mean 23); monotonic, roughly linear speed-up through 0.25/0.5/0.75/1 — per-ball px/frame [0.76,2.11,2.08] -> [1.50,4.02,3.85] -> [1.87,6.19,5.35] -> [2.75,7.66,7.58].
dials.portEffect: Same shape: 0 = frozen (motion 0, frame mean 26); monotonic speed-up — [4.50,2.58,0.55] -> [7.64,5.04,1.26] -> [5.12,7.15,2.06] -> [13.09,9.83,2.65]. Direction and rough linearity match, but the port's fast ball tops out ~1.7x above the original's fastest at every setting.

feedback: Narrow and re-centre the per-ball random speed range. At default BallSpeed, 20 fps, default 16x16 grid, the original's per-ball step spans 0.72-4.35 px/frame (median 2.91, n=63 balls over 21 seeds); the port spans 1.39-8.32 px/frame (median 3.27). Aim for an upper bound near 4.3 px/frame and a lower bound near 0.7 — a third of the port's balls currently exceed anything the original does, and the port never produces the original's slow, lazily drifting ball, which is a visible part of the original's character (there is almost always one ball crawling while the others zip).

Decouple ball velocity from the render frame rate, or scale it so it matches the original at the device's actual frame rate. The original advances a fixed step per rendered frame — its output at frame N is identical whether the engine runs at 10, 20 or 40 fps — while the port integrates elapsed time and so covers a constant distance per second. The two only agree near 20 fps; at 40 fps the original is ~2x faster than the port per frame and at 10 fps ~2x slower, so on hardware running faster than 20 fps the port will look noticeably sluggish next to the original.

The knock-on of the item above: at low frame rates the port degenerates. Rendered at 5 fps for 60 s the port's balls land on an exact per-frame cycle (red frame-mean pinned constant for all 300 frames) and the animation reads as flat strobing bands, while the original still reads as three balls bouncing. Fixing the per-frame stepping fixes this too.

Everything else is already right and should not be touched: blob falloff profile and radius (row through a red peak matches the original within a few counts at both BallRadius 0.5 and 1.0), the 1.0-14.0 px bounce bounds on a 16x16 grid, three balls one per primary, additive blending, per-ball strict periodicity with no re-randomisation over 1200 frames, and both sliders' names, kinds, endpoints and response curves.
